name: Electromagnetic wave field theory
summary: Maxwell's mathematical theory of electric and magnetic fields, which predicted waves travelling at the speed of light and so suggested light is electromagnetic.
description: A dynamical field formulation incorporates induction and electric displacement, yielding transverse disturbances with a calculated speed compared with optical measurements.
tier_reason: A unified electromagnetic framework supplies later wave experiments, radio and electrical/optical theory across generations.

impact.note: It changed what light and electricity were taken to be, and radio, electrical engineering and later physics across many societies rest on it.

why: Faraday's field ideas and measured electrical constants that gave a speed close to that of light invited a unified mathematical account.

market.note: Commercial availability is not a milestone of a scientific knowledge result.

date.basis: Received 27 October and read 8 December 1864; expanded paper published 1865.

events.statement: A dynamical field formulation incorporates induction and electric displacement, yielding transverse disturbances with a calculated speed compared with optical measurements.
events.caveats: The 1864 framework uses a mechanical medium and twenty equations; it is not identical to the modern four-equation notation. The contemporary abstract was inspected; the archival manuscript catalogue was unavailable, and the complete 1865 paper was not inspected.

evidence.supports: Field equations, named empirical foundations, transverse disturbances and light-speed comparison.
Establishes the 1864 receipt and presentation dates.

date.basis: Date of Lodge’s delivered lecture; not a claim of first recognition.

events.statement: Lodge credited Maxwell’s electromagnetic theory of light and discussed Hertz’s corroborating work before the Royal Institution.
events.caveats: Lodge states his own and his audience’s scientific recognition; it does not establish universal acceptance or that all had read the exact 1864 paper.

evidence.locator: Lecture introduction pp. 2–4 and discussion of electromagnetic theory of light
evidence.supports: Lodge explicitly credits and endorses Maxwell’s combined theory of light and electricity for his Royal Institution audience.

links.statement: Faraday’s investigations of induced currents supplied an explicitly acknowledged empirical foundation for Maxwell’s field equations.
links.scope: Maxwell’s 1864 formulation; the source endpoint represents the 1831 induction result.
links.alternatives: Felici’s investigations are acknowledged alongside Faraday; other empirical and mathematical inputs also appear.
links.caveats: Maxwell cites the research programme, not this ring apparatus alone; no exclusive causal role is assigned to the single configuration.
links.timing: The receiving development follows the source development.

evidence.locator: Printed p. 534, paragraph beginning These equations are founded
evidence.supports: Explicitly names Faraday and Felici’s induction investigations.
Establishes the transient induced-current result represented by the source node.

links.statement: Maxwell explicitly identifies Ørsted’s action of currents on a magnet as an empirical foundation of his field equations.
links.alternatives: The same paragraph names Faraday, Felici and Mossotti; this is one empirical input, not a sole ancestry.
links.caveats: None material for this bounded relationship.
links.timing: The receiving development follows the source development.

evidence.locator: Printed p. 534, paragraph beginning These equations are founded
evidence.supports: Names Ørsted’s observation as a foundation.

links.statement: Maxwell explicitly used Faraday’s magnetic rotation of polarized light, together with Thomson’s interpretation of that effect, to motivate motion in the medium of his 1864 electromagnetic field theory.
links.scope: The rationale in Maxwell’s 1864 abstract; the cited observation is Faraday’s magneto-optic rotation, not a claim that the particular glass specimen uniquely determined the theory.
links.alternatives: Maxwell also used induction, electric displacement, mechanical reasoning and other empirical results. He credited Thomson’s interpretation alongside Faraday’s observation.
links.caveats: The historical mechanical-medium interpretation is reported as Maxwell’s argument, not endorsed as a present physical mechanism. The specific heavy-glass specimen is not named in Maxwell’s abstract.
links.timing: Faraday’s 1845 reported result precedes Maxwell’s 1864 abstract. Community-entry display dates do not determine this historical relationship.

evidence.locator: Printed pp. 531–532 / PDF pp. 1–2, paragraph across page break and Thomson footnote
evidence.supports: Maxwell names Faraday’s rotation of the polarization plane by magnetic force, then uses Thomson’s medium-motion argument in his field rationale; both original pages visually inspected.
Establishes the magnetic polarization-rotation result represented by the source endpoint.
